title: The Modern Data Stack — Tool Landscape
summary: How the major tool categories in a data stack fit together, as a map before this curriculum goes deep on each layer in later groups.

slides.markdown:
Job postings list a dozen tool names — Fivetran, Airflow, dbt, Snowflake, Looker — and it's easy to mistake memorizing the list for understanding the stack. What actually matters is the **layer** each tool occupies and why that layer exists, because tools inside a layer are largely interchangeable while the layers themselves are not.

This topic is the map: five layers, what each is responsible for, and the buy-vs-build question that recurs at every one of them. Every later group in this curriculum — extraction, orchestration, transformation, warehousing — is a deep dive into exactly one of these layers.

![The modern data stack drawn as five layers with orchestration spanning all of them](assets/stack-layers.svg)

Orchestration is drawn differently on purpose — it's not a stage data passes *through*, it's the control plane that schedules and sequences every other layer.

assets.alt: The modern data stack drawn as five layers with orchestration spanning all of them

slides.markdown:
Managed ingestion tools (Fivetran, Airbyte, Stitch) offer pre-built connectors for common sources — Salesforce, Stripe, Postgres — handling pagination, rate limits, and schema drift for you, in exchange for a subscription cost that scales with data volume.

Hand-rolled extraction (a Python script hitting an API, a custom CDC connector) costs engineering time upfront and ongoing maintenance, but has no per-row pricing and gives full control over edge cases a managed tool's connector doesn't handle well.

The practical split: managed tools win for common, well-supported sources where the connector already exists and works — building your own Salesforce connector is rarely worth it. Hand-rolled wins for a source with no good managed connector, unusual volume/cost economics, or requirements (like exact-order delivery) a generic connector wasn't built for.

slides.sectionTitle: Orchestrators as the pipeline's control plane
slides.markdown:
An orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, Prefect) doesn't move or transform data itself — its job is deciding **when** each other layer's jobs run and **in what order**, based on a dependency graph.

Concretely: it knows that the dbt transform job can't start until the Fivetran sync has landed today's data, and that a downstream ML feature job depends on that transform finishing successfully. Without an orchestrator, that dependency logic lives in cron timing guesses ("the sync usually finishes by 3am, so schedule the transform at 4am") which silently breaks the first time the sync runs late.

This is why orchestration sits conceptually apart from the data-flow layers: it's infrastructure *about* the other infrastructure, and gets a full topic of its own next in the Batch Processing group.

slides.sectionTitle: Transformation: in the warehouse vs in a cluster
slides.markdown:
Two genuinely different transformation approaches coexist in most stacks:

- **In-warehouse (SQL/dbt-style)** — the transform runs as SQL, executed by the warehouse's own compute, on data already loaded there. This is push-down compute, and it's the default for most business-logic modeling: joins, aggregations, incremental models.
- **In-cluster (Spark)** — the transform runs on a separate distributed compute cluster, usually on data still sitting in a lake before or during load, or when the logic needs something SQL can't express cleanly.

Most modern ELT-style stacks lean heavily on the first, reaching for Spark specifically when a job needs custom code, ML feature engineering, or scale the warehouse's SQL engine handles less gracefully than a purpose-built cluster.

slides.sectionTitle: Warehouses and lakehouses as the system of record
slides.markdown:
A **warehouse** (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) is a managed, columnar-storage analytical database — you load data into it and it handles storage layout and query execution together. A **lakehouse** (Databricks with Delta Lake, or S3 + Iceberg/Hudi) separates storage (cheap object storage) from compute (a query engine that reads it), aiming for warehouse-like query performance and transactional guarantees on top of lake-cheap storage.

Either way, this layer is where curated, business-meaningful tables live — the thing every BI tool and most ML feature pipelines ultimately query. The engine-internals detail of how this layer executes fast columnar scans is its own group later; here the point is just: this is the layer everything else in the stack exists to feed correctly and on time.

| Layer | "Buy" example | "Build" example | Buy wins when | Build wins when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ingestion** | Fivetran connector | Custom Python extractor | Common source, standard needs | Unusual source or cost economics |
| **Orchestration** | Managed Airflow (MWAA, Astronomer) | Self-hosted Airflow/Dagster | Team doesn't want to run infra | Need deep customization or cost control at scale |
| **Warehouse** | Snowflake/BigQuery (fully managed) | Self-managed lakehouse on S3 | Want zero ops overhead | Need storage/compute cost separation at large scale |
| **Transform** | dbt Cloud | Self-hosted dbt-core + CI | Small team, wants managed scheduling/docs | Cost-sensitive, already has CI infra |

The real trade at every row is the same: money and vendor dependency versus engineering time and operational ownership. Neither answer is universally right — it tracks team size, existing infra, and how much the workload actually differs from the common case a vendor optimized for.

slides.sectionTitle: Adopting big-data tools at small-data scale
slides.markdown:
A recurring mistake: adopting Kafka or Spark "for the future" when the current dataset comfortably fits in a single warehouse query or a Pandas script.

Spark's value comes from distributing computation across many machines — if your dataset is a few GB and fits in memory on one machine, a Spark cluster adds coordination overhead (task scheduling, shuffling data between workers) that a single-node job simply doesn't pay, and you'll likely see it run *slower* than the "simple" alternative while costing more to operate. Kafka's value comes from durable, ordered, replayable event streaming at high throughput — a system with a few thousand events a day gets none of that benefit and pays for cluster operations, partition management, and a new skill set the team now has to maintain.

The tell is the same as elsewhere in this curriculum: adopt a tool for a scale problem you actually have, verified with real numbers, not one you're forecasting might exist in two years.

This topic's job was breadth, not depth — every one of these five layers gets a real deep dive elsewhere in the curriculum: extraction patterns and CDC for ingestion, orchestration and idempotency for the control plane, dbt-style modeling for transformation, and columnar storage internals for the warehouse layer.

The habit worth keeping from here forward: when you meet a new tool, place it on this map first — what layer does it occupy, and what's it competing against inside that layer — before evaluating whether it's good. A tool that's excellent at ingestion tells you nothing about whether it's the right transformation choice, because those are different jobs with different success criteria entirely.
